During a short break in a long trial, the judges and lawyers of the Law Courts gathered in a private room, where one of them opened a newspaper and read aloud that Ivan Ilyich Golovin had died. <break time="0.8s" /> Upon hearing the news, each man present thought first not of the colleague he had lost but of the vacant post, and of the promotions and transfers that it might bring to himself or to his friends. <break time="0.8s" /> Beneath these calculations lay another feeling, which none of them would admit, a quiet relief that the one who had died at forty five was Ivan Ilyich and not themselves. <break time="0.8s" /> His old friend Pyotr Ivanovich went to the house that evening, and although he had meant to share the familys grief, he found himself thinking less about the dead man than about the evenings card game. <break time="0.8s" /> In the drawing room, the widow, Praskovya Fyodorovna, spoke at length of her own suffering during her husbands illness and then asked, in the same tone, how she might obtain more money from the government. <break time="0.8s" /> So absorbed was she in these practical matters that Pyotr Ivanovich, sitting awkwardly on a low stool with broken springs, began to feel that his words of comfort were hardly needed. <break time="0.8s" /> As he was leaving, he met Gerasim, the young servant who had cared for his master to the end, and Gerasim said simply that it was Gods will and that all of us must come to it one day. <break time="0.8s" /> Stepping out into the fresh night air, Pyotr Ivanovich felt as if he had escaped something unpleasant, and he hurried off, hoping that he might still be in time for the card game.

Ivan Ilyichs life had been most simple and most ordinary, and for that very reason, as the rest of the story slowly and painfully reveals, it had also been most terrible. <break time="0.8s" /> The son of an official, he studied law, took up a modest post in the provinces, and quickly learned to do whatever was considered proper by the people of high rank around him. <break time="0.8s" /> Like a fly drawn toward the light, he was drawn toward those who stood above him, adopting their manners and their views without ever asking whether they were truly right. <break time="0.8s" /> He married Praskovya Fyodorovna, a pretty girl of good family, not so much because he loved her deeply as because the marriage was pleasant to him and was approved by the right people. <break time="0.8s" /> When his wife grew jealous and demanding during her first pregnancy, he did not try to understand her but withdrew, little by little, into his work, where everything was orderly and under his control. <break time="0.8s" /> In court, he learned to strip away everything human from a case, reducing living people to documents and forms, so that he could deal with them coolly while still appearing polite and fair. <break time="0.8s" /> Thus his years passed, lightly, pleasantly, and decently, filled with official duties, comfortable dinners, and evening games of cards, and it never occurred to him that anything essential might be missing.

What tormented Ivan Ilyich most was the lie, accepted by everyone around him, that he was only ill and not dying, and that he needed nothing more than rest and medicine to recover. <break time="0.8s" /> Only Gerasim, a fresh faced young peasant who had come to serve in the house, did not lie, and he performed even the most unpleasant tasks for his master lightly and without any sign of disgust. <break time="0.8s" /> When Ivan Ilyich found that his pain eased if his legs were raised, Gerasim sat for hours holding them on his shoulders, and in that position the sick man found a comfort that no doctor had given him. <break time="0.8s" /> When his master apologized for the trouble, Gerasim answered with a calm smile, We will all die someday, so why should I not take a little trouble for you. <break time="0.8s" /> Ivan Ilyich understood that Gerasim alone pitied him, and he longed, though he was ashamed to admit it, to be petted and comforted like a sick child, which was exactly what no one else would do. <break time="0.8s" /> One evening his wife and daughter, dressed in their finest clothes, came in to see him before going to the theater, where a famous French actress was performing, and their healthy, perfumed presence felt like an insult. <break time="0.8s" /> Later, alone in the dark, he wept like a child over his helplessness, his loneliness, and the cruelty of people and of God, demanding to know why he had been made to suffer so much. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, as he grew quiet, he seemed to hear the voice of his own soul asking what he really wanted, and he answered that he wanted to live, to live well and pleasantly, as he had before.

As he recalled his past, Ivan Ilyich noticed a strange pattern, for the further back he went into his childhood, the more real joy he found, while the later years of success seemed ever emptier. <break time="0.8s" /> Then came a question he had always driven away, a question so terrible that he could hardly bear to face it, namely whether his whole life had been, in fact, entirely wrong. <break time="0.8s" /> He had defended his correct and respectable life against this doubt, but now, looking at the faces of his wife and the doctor, he saw in them everything he had lived by, and it was all a deception. <break time="0.8s" /> For three days he struggled, as if someone were pushing him into a narrow black sack, and what held him back was not the darkness itself but his belief that his life had been a good one. <break time="0.8s" /> At the very end of the third day, his young son crept quietly to the bedside, and Ivan Ilyich, feeling the boys tears and kiss upon his hand, suddenly felt sorry for him. <break time="0.8s" /> At that same moment he broke through into a light, and he understood that although his life had not been what it should have been, it was still possible to set it right. <break time="0.8s" /> Looking at his weeping wife and son with pity, he wished to free them from his suffering, and he tried to say Forgive, but the word came out wrong, and he simply let it go. <break time="0.8s" /> Searching for his old fear of death, he could no longer find it, for where death had been there was only light, and he said to himself, Death is finished, it is no more.
